stories.headline: Keralite vlogger, who claimed arrest by Mujahideen, now says she escaped arrest threat in Afghanistan
stories.deck: "According to the law of this country, a woman cannot travel alone," the vlogger, who runs the Facebook page Backpacker Arunima, said in a fresh social media post. She added that she had earlier been denied a permit in Jalalabad because she was travelling alone
stories.bodyText:
A woman travel vlogger from Keralam, who had earlier claimed that she was arrested by the "Mujahideen" in Afghanistan, has now said that local authorities threatened to arrest her in Bamyan, citing the country's law that women cannot travel without a male companion or guide.
"According to the law of this country, a woman cannot travel alone," the vlogger, who runs the Facebook page Backpacker Arunima, said in a fresh social media post. She added that she had earlier been denied a permit in Jalalabad because she was travelling alone.
The authorities in Bamyan told her that she had violated the law and would be arrested, the vlogger claimed.
Recounting the incident, she said she reached Bamyan around 7 p.m. and was questioned about her passport, visa and permit.
She became extremely frightened after being told that she had violated the law. So she contacted a man who had earlier helped her reach Bamyan, and he spoke to the authorities on her behalf, the vlogger said.
According to her account, the authorities insisted that she obtain a permit and travel with a guide. She said she was eventually allowed to proceed towards the next country after discussions.
"I had to go through all this only because I am a woman," the vlogger said, adding that she planned to travel around 500 kilometres towards the Uzbekistan border and expected to encounter several checkpoints on the way.
The woman said she was extremely frightened and feared that something might happen to her, and hence posted an Instagram story hoping that someone would come to her rescue.
In an earlier post, she had sought help to contact the Indian embassy, saying, "I am in trouble in Afghanistan. I am in Bamyan." In the post, she had also shared what she described as a translation of an official communication from local authorities, according to which she had been arrested by the "Mujahideen".
PTI could not independently verify her claims.

stories.headline: 'He said stop bike': Gurgaon woman biker recounts moments before car hits her
stories.deck: A young woman fell from her superbike after a car allegedly cut her path. She narrowly escaped being run over by fast-moving traffic on Golf Course Road. Action camera footage captured the incident and its immediate aftermath. The driver of the Maruti Ciaz offered a different account of the events. The woman later shared the footage on social media platforms.
stories.bodyText:
GURGAON: A young woman was thrown off her superbike on Sunday after a man riding a car allegedly cut across her path, leaving her dangerously exposed to fast-moving traffic as she fell in the middle of Golf Course Road. The biker, scrambling for safety, narrowly escaped being run over as vehicles swept past her.
The 
road rage
 was captured by an action camera mounted on the handle of her Aprilia RS 457. The footage the woman later shared on social media showed the moments leading up to the collision and what followed. The Maruti Ciaz driver gave a contrasting account of what led to the collision.
Shivani Chauhan, who identified herself as Sia in the video, said she was riding with a group towards The Biker’s Barn cafe when the man driving the car (HR30Y4949) began following her on Sunday morning. She alleged its occupants repeatedly tried to catch up with her and asked her to pull over.
“I told him to drive a little farther away. And he said, ‘stop the bike,’” she said in the video, adding that she suspected the occupants were drunk. She said she accelerated to stay ahead and prevent the car from cutting across her path.
A friend riding behind also tried to shield her, placing his motorcycle between the Ciaz and Shivani as the car continued to make aggressive manoeuvres and tried to get alongside Shivani, repeatedly attempting to cut in front of her bike.
He eventually succeeded in hitting her from the side. As the impact threw Shivani to the road, her motorcycle slid across the tar, the friction causing sparks that are visible in the video too. As the Ciaz drove away, one of her friends chased it and caught up with it at a traffic signal ahead. He confronted the driver and tried to open his door, asking him to step out. The driver denied responsibility and fled from the signal, Shivani alleged.
Kalyan Baisla of Palwal, the car driver, claimed a group of 22-23 bikers was riding aggressively, repeatedly overtaking his car and slowing down in front of it. Contrary to what the video suggests, he said Shivani suddenly turned while he was taking a U-turn, leaving him with little time to react. “She suddenly turned the vehicle without looking into the mirror. I could not control the car. Yet, I tried very hard to avoid the collision,” he added.
Baisla also denied fleeing after the accident. He said he rolled down his window when other bikers stopped him at the signal and told them he was not at fault. He further claimed that the video circulating on social media had been edited by joining separate clips. “They are playing the victim card. I did not hit them deliberately,” he said.
Shivani’s father Roshan Chauhan said she is a Delhi resident and social worker associated with Aam Aadmi Party. Chauhan, himself an AAP worker, said the family learnt about the crash on Monday because Shivani hadn’t told them anything about it. “I got to know about my daughter’s accident on Monday,” said Chauhan. He demanded that an attempt to murder case be filed against the accused.
Police took suo motu cognisance of the video and got an FIR registered on Monday. Till late in the evening, Shivani was yet to file a complaint.
“We have seen the video and registered an FIR at Sector 56 police station. The victim was contacted by police, but she’s yet to file a complaint. We will, however, examine the evidence and sequence of events that led to the crash,” ACP Abhilaksh Joshi said.
The FIR, based on a complaint by ASI Kuldeep Singh, has been registered against unknown persons under sections 125 (rash or negligent acts endangering human life or personal safety) and 281 (rash driving) of BNS. Singh said the accident occurred near Sector 55-56 Rapid Metro station. According to police, further sections would be considered after Shivani’s complaint and a medical report. “We will add more sections in the case following the complaint and medical report of the victim. The accused will be nabbed soon,” the SHO said.
The Ciaz was traced to its owner, Manish, who said he’s in the Army and was away on duty when his friend borrowed the car for two days. “My friend Kalyan Baisla took my car for some work two days ago. And now, he is not taking my calls,” he added.
Police sources said Baisla runs a gym and describes himself on social media as an international kabaddi and rugby player. Manish’s uncle Kartar Poshwal said the family came to know from neighbours that the car was involved in the crash. “Neither has our vehicle come back to us nor is Kalyan reachable,” he added.
Shivani declined to speak to the media and subsequently made her social media account private. She, however, said she would approach police with her lawyer and file a complaint. Singh in his complaint alleged that the accident happened near Sector 55-56 Rapid Metro station as he saw in the video on social media in which a car driver was seen ramming into a bike.

stories.headline: Gavaskar urges BCCI to make big change, names Sachin, Dravid for key role
stories.deck: Sunil Gavaskar has put forth a suggestion to enhance the BCCI's Cricket Advisory Committee by expanding its scope. He proposes that legendary former cricketers be included to ensure diverse perspectives. This broader committee could effectively tackle challenges related to both domestic and international cricket scheduling. Moreover, involving icons like Sachin Tendulkar would considerably…
stories.bodyText:
Sunil Gavaskar believes the 
BCCI
 needs to rethink the role of its Cricket Advisory Committee (CAC), suggesting that the panel should have a far wider mandate and draw on the experience of some of India's most celebrated former cricketers.
The former India captain's call comes after he criticised East Zone's approach in the Duleep Trophy final, where Ishan Kishan's side settled for the title on the basis of a first-innings lead. Gavaskar has previously expressed his dissatisfaction with the rule, which has continued to attract criticism over several domestic seasons.
According to Gavaskar, the CAC could play a much larger role in addressing such issues and shaping the future of Indian cricket.
Gavaskar wants bigger role for CAC
The current CAC appointments date back to 2022, when Ashok Malhotra, Jatin Paranjape and Sulakshana Naik were named to the three-member panel. Its traditional responsibilities have centred on selecting the head coach and national selectors, with the committee also conducting interviews for those positions.
However, there is uncertainty over whether the CAC still exists in its current form or has been disbanded.
Gavaskar believes the BCCI should instead broaden the committee's remit to cover wider aspects of the game, including domestic and international scheduling.
"There are no longer any committees in BCCI today apart from the selection committees and the CAC. Perhaps the time has come to expand the CAC and its brief of selecting the selectors and coach, and also look at fixtures — domestic and international, and all things related to Indian cricket. There are some incredibly experienced former cricketers whose expertise can be utilised to be on this committee," Gavaskar wrote in his column for the Mid-Day.
He also suggested a star-studded list of former India players who could contribute to such a panel.
"How about names like Sachin Tendulkar, Rahul Dravid, Sourav Ganguly, Ravi Shastri, Anil Kumble, Harbhajan Singh, 
Virender Sehwag
 — to name a few? The President and Secretary will be there too," he added.
'It carries a heft beyond measure'
Gavaskar believes involving former greats such as Tendulkar and Dravid in discussions with India's coaching and development setup could bring an additional level of expertise and authority.
"When this committee interacts with the coach and captain and the head of the NCA, it carries a heft beyond measure. A similar committee for women’s cricket, too, where experience and expertise meet to take calls to take Indian cricket forward," wrote Gavaskar.
The former batter, who also captained India to the 1985 Championship win, wants the idea to extend beyond the men's game, with a comparable advisory structure for women's cricket.
"Just thinking about this gives one the goosebumps. Will it ever happen, or is it just a dream?" he concluded.

stories.headline: Air India gets show-cause notice over Italian passengers skipping immigration at Delhi airport
stories.deck: The three passengers had taken a flight from Amritsar to Delhi on September 4 and subsequently boarded a Lufthansa flight from Delhi to Munich.
stories.bodyText:
The Civil Aviation Ministry has issued a show-cause notice to Air India for alleged procedural lapses that resulted in three Italian passengers taking a connecting flight from the Delhi airport without completing the immigration process earlier this month, and the Home Ministry has called for a meeting of the stakeholders to discuss the incident on Tuesday (September 15, 2026), according to sources.
The three passengers had taken a flight from Amritsar to Delhi on September 4 and subsequently boarded a Lufthansa flight from Delhi to Munich.
However, they did not complete the immigration process at the Delhi airport, the sources said.
There was no comment from Air India on the incident.
The Ministry has issued a show-cause notice to Air India CEO Campbell Wilson seeking an explanation for the alleged procedural lapses. 
The sources said Home Secretary Govind Mohan will chair a meeting to discuss the incident on Tuesday (September 15).
Secretary and Additional Secretary at the Civil Aviation Ministry, Director of the Intelligence Bureau, Additional Secretary (UT and Foreigners) at the Home Ministry, Bureau of Immigration (BoI) Commissioner, Air India CEO and Delhi Airport CEO are expected to attend the meeting, they added.
Amritsar airport is among the airports from where Air India has introduced 'Hub-and-Spoke' model flights, under which passengers can complete the immigration process at the origin airport and travel seamlessly to overseas destinations. At the hub airport from where the international flight starts, passengers can just go through the security check and board the flight concerned.
If a person is travelling from Amritsar via Delhi to a foreign destination, then Amritsar is the spoke and Delhi is the hub.
In the particular case of the three Italian passengers, the sources said they were issued the boarding passes at Amritsar airport for Delhi as well as the Lufthansa flight to Munich.
Since the two flights did not come under Air India's 'Hub-and-Spoke' model, the three passengers were supposed to come out through the arrival area and then do their immigration process before taking the Lufthansa flight.
However, after landing at the Delhi airport, they were taken to the international transfer area as a result of which they did not reach the immigration counter and without completing the immigration process took the flight to Munich, the sources said.
Air India and Lufthansa have an interline partnership. Generally, an interline agreement allows passengers to book connecting flights across different airlines under a single itinerary.

briefs.headline: U.S. lawmaker submits amendment naming India in Russia sanctions act
briefs.deck: The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, passed by the U.S. Senate by an overwhelming 86-11 vote last month, seeks to impose sanctions not only on Russia's leadership and energy sector but also on the "shadow fleet" of vessels that enable Moscow to evade sanctions on oil deliveries.
briefs.bodyText:
Racing against time, U.S. lawmakers submitted amendments to the Russia sanctions Bill, with one seeking to name its top trading partners — including India — in the legislation, and another proposing to scrap the section imposing tariffs altogether.
Also Read | U.S. Senate passes Russia sanctions bill that seeks 100% tariffs on India, four others
The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, passed by the U.S. Senate by an overwhelming 86-11 vote last month, seeks to impose sanctions not only on Russia's leadership and energy sector but also on the "shadow fleet" of vessels that enable Moscow to evade sanctions on oil deliveries.
The U.S. believes that Russia's crude oil trade is funding the war against Ukraine. The Bill also seeks to authorise President Donald Trump to impose 100% tariffs on Russia's top oil trading partners, including China and India.
The Bill passed by the U.S. Senate on August 7 does not name Russia's trading partners but does mention the five largest importers of oil and gas by volume.
The House of Representatives must pass the bill before sending it to the President for signature. The House has four working days left before it breaks into early recess ahead of the midterm elections on November 3.
The amendment moved by Democratic Congressman Steny Hoyer seeks to name China, India, Turkiye, Azerbaijan, Hungary, the Slovak Republic, the UAE, Singapore, Kazakhstan, and the Kyrgyz Republic as countries eligible for 100% duties.
Interestingly, Democratic Congressman Gregory Meeks, who is staunchly opposed to granting more tariff-levying powers to Mr. Trump, has moved an amendment to scrap the entire Section 113 that seeks to grant authority to the President to impose broad secondary tariffs on Russia's trading partners.
The amendment moved by Meeks has three co-sponsors.
The amendments to the Russia sanctions act were made public by the House Rules Committee on Monday (September 14, 2026).
Another amendment moved by Meeks seeks to allow the President to waive the sanctions applicable to a foreign person for a period of 90 days, with a provision for renewal for additional periods of 90 days, if it is "vital to the national security of the US." Meeks has also moved an amendment seeking to authorise $15 billion in direct loans to Ukraine for financing the procurement of defence articles and services.

briefs.headline: Drone shot down by NATO over Lithuania
briefs.deck: Baltic states Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia — NATO members sharing a long border with Russia — regularly report drone incursions into their territories as part of Moscow's war with Ukraine.
briefs.bodyText:
NATO fighter jets shot down a drone over Lithuania, the country's President Gitanas Nauseda said on Tuesday (September 15, 2026).
Baltic states Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia — NATO members sharing a long border with Russia — regularly report drone incursions into their territories as part of Moscow's war with Ukraine.
"A drone that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed by NATO fighter jets," Mr. Nauseda wrote in a post on X.
"With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region," he added.
According to Lithuanian public radio LRT, which cited the National Crisis Management Center (NKVC), the drone crashed in a rural area near Lake Kaunas, in the country's central region.
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys in a post on X thanked allies "whose presence helps protect our skies and strengthens our security".
"This is best example of Allied unity and resolve in action — sending a clear message that NATO stands vigilant, committed, and ready," he added.
A NATO fighter shot down a Ukrainian drone over Estonia in May, the first interception of a foreign drone in the airspace of a Baltic state by NATO's air police since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Published - September 15, 2026 06:34 am IST

briefs.headline: Bamboo mass flowering and die-off can trigger ecological crisis and wildlife conflict, study warns
briefs.deck: Synchronous flowering and die-off can open the door to invasive weeds, fuel wildfires, trigger rodent surges and push elephants into farmland, says Kerala Forest Research Institute study
briefs.bodyText:
The synchronous mass flowering and subsequent die-off of bamboo across forest landscapes can trigger a chain of ecological shocks — from invasive weed outbreaks and intense wildfires to rodent population explosions and spikes in human-elephant conflict, a study by Dr. T.V. Sajeev of the Kerala Forest Research Institute (KFRI), Peechi, Thrissur, Keralam, has warned.
Published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution, the study calls for forest departments to move from reactive crisis management to anticipatory, landscape-level planning, particularly in fragmented ecosystems such as the Western Ghats.
“Woody bamboos are vital to tropical forests, helping regulate microclimates and carbon cycles. But their monocarpic life cycle ends in a dramatic event. After flowering at intervals ranging from 40 to more than 120 years, entire bamboo cohorts flower, senesce and die together, sometimes across hundreds or thousands of square kilometres.,” points out Dr. Sajeev
When the canopy collapses
The first shock comes with the sudden disappearance of the bamboo canopy.
Dense bamboo stands normally intercept most incoming solar energy, allowing only 2% to 5% of photosynthetically active radiation to reach the understory. When an entire cohort dies, the canopy collapses, exposing large areas of the forest floor.
These extensive light gaps raise topsoil temperatures, speed up moisture loss and trigger rapid nutrient mineralisation. The openings then become prime sites for opportunistic invasive plants. Instead of native climax tree species regenerating, invasive weeds such as Senna spectabilis, Mikania micrantha and Lantana camara can quickly take over, he notes.
The study highlights Senna spectabilis, an invasive tree that heavily infests protected reserves in southern India. Its fallen foliage releases toxic secondary metabolites, mainly phenolics, fatty acids and terpenoids, into moist soil.
Under the “novel weapons hypothesis”, these phytochemicals can suppress antioxidant enzyme activity and cause lipid peroxidation in the roots of native plants. This gives Senna an advantage, suppressing the natural seed bank and preventing bamboo seedlings from establishing.
“The result can be a permanent shift from open forest gaps to degraded, invasive-dominated thickets, as seen in the Wayanad landscape,” says Dr Sajeev.
Elephants pushed towards farms
The loss of bamboo also creates a major food crisis for primary consumers, particularly Asian elephants (Elephas maximus).
Bamboo is an important high-volume food source for elephants, especially during lean dry seasons. When vast stands die and the understory becomes dominated by dense, unpalatable and physically impenetrable Senna and Lantana thickets, elephants face severe forage shortages.
“Driven by the need to find food, herds can expand their ranges and travel greater distances. This can push them beyond protected-area boundaries and into agricultural fringes. The result is a sharp rise in human-elephant conflict, including crop losses, property damage and threats to human life. Repeated losses can also erode the goodwill of communities living around forests towards wildlife conservation,” the study points out.
Seeds trigger rodent surges
Bamboo masting brings another unexpected consequence: a massive food bonanza for rodents.
Dr. Sajeev notes that gregarious flowering can carpet the forest floor with carbohydrate-rich bamboo seeds, sometimes producing thousands of kilograms of seed biomass per hectare. The abundance of food can cause explosive population growth among granivorous rodents such as Rattus and Melomys species.
Once the forest seed supply is exhausted or decays, the enlarged rodent populations can move into neighbouring croplands and grain stores.
Drawing parallels with historical Mautam famines in northeast India, the study warns that such rodent irruptions can cause extensive agricultural losses and increase the risk of zoonotic infections, including scrub typhus and hantaviruses, among rural communities, he warns.
Dead bamboo creates fire danger
The mass death of bamboo also transforms the forest into a potential tinderbox.
Millions of metric tonnes of dead, hollow culms can accumulate on the forest floor. During dry seasons, this continuous layer of dry biomass creates a huge fuel load capable of supporting high-intensity wildfires.
“Such fires can destroy vulnerable bamboo seedlings, burn soil organic matter and volatilise topsoil nutrients. This can create a self-reinforcing degradation cycle in which fire-adapted invasive weeds gain ground while native forest recovery suffers,” the study points out.
Prepare before the crisis
The study urges wildlife and forest authorities to anticipate these cascading impacts rather than respond after the crisis begins.
It recommends maintaining bamboo stands of multiple lineages so that large tracts do not flower and collapse simultaneously.
It also calls for targeted, pre-emptive clearing of dead bamboo culms along vulnerable stretches before the dry season, reducing fuel continuity and wildfire risk.
In newly formed canopy gaps, authorities should immediately undertake manual or targeted eradication of alien invasive species before their allelopathic compounds become established in the rhizosphere and further suppress native regeneration.
For elephants, the study recommends landscape-scale planning to identify and strictly protect temporary compensatory foraging and movement corridors. These alternative pathways can provide displaced herds with adequate forage and help steer them away from vulnerable farming belts during the multi-year transition following a masting event.
The study warns that bamboo mass flowering should not be dismissed as merely a periodic botanical spectacle. When an entire bamboo landscape flowers and dies together, the ecological consequences can ripple far beyond the forest — reaching farms, wildlife and human communities.

briefs.headline: 'Are they living in the past?': Ex-India cricketer slams Mohsin Naqvi
briefs.deck: The celebration of India's Women's Asia Cup triumph was overshadowed when the team rejected the trophy presented by ACC president Mohsin Naqvi. This decision recalls a similar controversy during the men's Asia Cup final. Mohammad Kaif has voiced doubts regarding Naqvi's involvement in both political and sports spheres, reflecting wider issues related to his dual authority in the cricketing…
briefs.bodyText:
India's Women's Asia Cup triumph in Dubai was overshadowed by another awkward trophy presentation involving Asian Cricket Council president Mohsin Naqvi, as the champions once again declined to collect the silverware from the Pakistan Cricket Board chief.
India defeated Sri Lanka by 72 runs in the final on Sunday to claim the title, but the post-match ceremony was held up amid the standoff. Naqvi, who is also 
Pakistan
's Interior Minister, remained at the venue, but India's players were unwilling to receive the trophy from him.
The episode was strikingly similar to last year's men's Asia Cup final, when India's victorious team had also refused to accept the trophy from Naqvi. The repeat has once again put the spotlight on his dual role as a senior cricket administrator and a prominent figure in Pakistan's government.
Mohammad Kaif questions Naqvi's dual responsibilities
Former India batter Mohammad Kaif has questioned whether Naqvi can give sufficient attention to cricket administration while simultaneously handling major political responsibilities.
“Are they living in the past? Don't they have a reality check? Mohsin Naqvi is in politics. He is the boss of the board. It's not like that,” Kaif said on Cricbuzz.
“If you are in cricket, then you have to be in cricket. You have to go to two places. 
It's a difficult job. You won't be able to give time. You have so many political commitments. You have to run the cricket board. You have to see what's going on inside. You have to stop at one place and invest time. If you look at any body, if you compare it with the BCCI, or look at it from the outside, nobody does two things.”
Naqvi's responsibilities extend beyond the PCB. As ACC president, PCB chairman and Pakistan's Interior Minister, he occupies influential positions across both cricket and government, making his involvement in major India-Pakistan cricket events particularly sensitive.
Kaif believes leading a cricket board demands a level of focus that can be difficult to provide while holding another major office.
“Either you are a politician, or you are a cricketer. You have to balance it. You have to focus on one thing,” he said.
Kaif also rejected the idea that Pakistan's cricketing problems stem from a lack of talented players.
According to the former India international, Pakistan continues to possess considerable natural ability but needs a better system and the right people to turn that talent into successful professional cricketers.
“Players aren't bad. You need people who make players. There is a lot of talent in Pakistan,” he added.
The latest controversy has ensured that India's Women's Asia Cup victory will be remembered for more than the 72-run win over Sri Lanka. Instead of a routine trophy celebration, the final once again ended with an unresolved presentation involving Naqvi.
With a similar situation having played out at the men's Asia Cup final last year, questions over Naqvi's role at the intersection of cricket administration and politics are likely to remain part of the conversation.

briefs.headline: Trump says there is ‘SICK conspiracy’ against AI and data centres, dismisses new guardrails
briefs.deck: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Mr. Trump said
briefs.bodyText:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday (September 14, 2026) that he would be a sufficient guardrail against rogue artificial intelligence, claiming that any efforts to limit the technology was part of a “SICK conspiracy.”
Mr. Trump was pushing back against calls by tech leaders such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk to have greater government oversight of AI. Their goal is to ensure the technology is developed in ways that promote safety, address legal liability, feed economic growth, advance science and preserve national security.
The president maintained that his presence in the Oval Office should assuage any fears about AI, which has become a source of controversy after a series of hacks in recent months that showed AI agents could be working to deceive humans.
“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Mr. Trump posted on social media.
Mr. Trump specifically said that the administration has already stopped the AI company Anthropic “from doing bad, or potentially bad” things. Anthropic has endured an uncomfortable relationship with the Trump administration, with the Pentagon trying to label the company’s models a security risk and a temporary ban of one of its more advanced models.
Mr. Amodei published a 3,800-word essay on Saturday (September 12, 2026) that called for slower development of AI. Microsoft on Monday (September 14, 2026) published its own code of conduct to ensure that humans control AI. The actions come after a series of warnings by AI experts about the technologies’ capabilities and the July 2026 cyberattack by OpenAI models on the AI company Hugging Face.
But the president has opposed such efforts to constrain AI and claims that doing so could cause China to eclipse America on AI.
“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China,” Mr. Trump said.
The president has long resisted efforts for greater government oversight of AI, embracing his philosophy going back to 2016 of “I alone can fix it.” He returned to the White House last year by revoking a Biden administration executive order on AI oversight and only providing a fuller order of his own more than 16 months later this past June.
The prospect of slower AI buildout led stocks to slip in Monday (September 14, 2026) morning trading, as demand for advanced computer chips and construction materials for data centres could fall. But Mr. Trump’s frustration comes as AI has also emerged as a political liability ahead of November’s midterm elections, with many voters opposing the construction of additional data centres and expressing worries that AI could lead to job losses and undermine the education of children.
Rahm Emanuel, the former Chicago mayor, Democratic congressman and White House chief of staff, said on Saturday (September 12, 2026) that the Anthropic CEO’s essay was “an admission that we’re driving down a dark, winding road on wet pavement with the headlights off. And where’s President Trump? Looks like he nodded off again. It’s time to turn the lights on, put both hands on the wheel, and regain control before it’s too late.”
But the administration has repeatedly sought to minimise the risks being highlighted by AI companies.
Vice-President J.D. Vance told reporters Monday (September 14, 2026) morning about AI, “I don’t think Americans should be scared of anything.”
Mr. Vance, speaking as he prepared to fly to Kansas for a midterm election campaign event, said that the Trump administration is concerned about AI but wants to make sure it is regulating the technology smartly, warning that the U.S. is in an AI arms race against China.
“Personally, I feel a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them. It feels a little bit to me like a bit of a Trojan horse,” Mr. Vance said. “So, I think we just have to be careful about this.”
Published - September 14, 2026 10:09 pm IST

briefs.headline: Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations begin with fervour across Telangana
briefs.deck: Lakhs of Lord Ganesha idols of various sizes and forms were installed at homes, apartment complexes and road corners for worship in Hyderabad and all other towns and villages in the State
briefs.bodyText:
The nine-day Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations began with devotional fervour and gaiety across Telangana on Monday (September 14, 2026).
Lakhs of Lord Ganesha idols of various sizes and forms were installed at homes, apartment complexes and road corners for worship in Hyderabad and all other towns and villages in the State.
Hyderabad residents woke up to a pleasant morning following overnight drizzle in the city and visited markets to purchase idols and other puja material.
Devotees thronged temples and offered prayers at homes on the occasion of Ganesh Chaturthi, known as Vinayaka Chavithi in Telangana and neighbouring Andhra Pradesh.
The major attraction of the Ganesh Chaturthi in the State was the giant-sized Ganesh idol installed at the pandal at Khairatabad in Hyderabad.
This year a 69-ft tall idol has been installed at the Khairatabad pandal. The idol has been named as 'Pancha Mukha Sankata Hara Maha Ganapati' wishing for removal of devotees' obstacles.
Telangana Governor Shiv Pratap Shukla offered prayers at the giant idol of Ganapati and wished that Lord Ganesha shower his blessings on all.
The government and police made elaborate arrangements, including for security, to ensure smooth conduct of the festivities.
The idols would be immersed in water bodies following the nine-day festivities. Thousands of idols would be immersed in the Hussain Sagar lake and other lakes and tanks in Hyderabad.
The Governor, Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy, Union Ministers G. Kishan Reddy and Bandi Sanjay Kumar and leaders of all major parties wished devotees on the occasion of Ganesh Chaturthi.
Published - September 14, 2026 02:09 pm IST

briefs.headline: What are the AI threats flagged by Anthropic? | Explained
briefs.deck: Anthropic released information about several malicious activities detected and disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026, which had serious implications across seven key areas: scams and fraud, cyber operations, illicit distillation, influence operations, surveillance operations, conventional weapons and biological misuse
briefs.bodyText:
Amid heightened debates about threats from and responsible use of artificial intelligence, Anthropic, the research-based U.S. company behind the Claude family of large language models and other AI products, has released several cases of misuse of its systems, warning of growing risks as AI models become more capable.
In a 154-page report published on Thursday (September 10, 2026), the firm released information about several malicious activities detected and disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026, which had serious implications across seven key areas: scams and fraud, cyber operations, illicit distillation, influence operations, surveillance operations, conventional weapons and biological misuse. The actors behind the detected misuse included suspected state-sponsored groups, financially motivated criminals, state propaganda institutions and politically motivated individuals.

briefs.headline: Former DUTA chief Aditya Narayan Mishra joins Congress, flags ‘crisis’ in education
briefs.deck: Mr. Mishra joined the party in the presence of Delhi Congress in-charge Qazi Nizamuddin, Delhi Pradesh Congress Committee president Devender Yadav, AICC Uttar Pradesh in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam and other party leaders
briefs.bodyText:
Former Delhi University Teachers Association (DUTA) president Aditya Narayan Mishra, who has headed the teachers’ body three times, joined the Congress on Monday (September 14, 2026) along with some other academicians, saying the country’s education system was facing a serious crisis.
The organisation Academics for Action and Development (AAD) was also formally merged with the Congress.
Mr. Mishra joined the party in the presence of Delhi Congress in-charge Qazi Nizamuddin, Delhi Pradesh Congress Committee president Devender Yadav, AICC Uttar Pradesh in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam and other party leaders. He has also served as president of the Federation of Central Universities Teachers Associations.
Welcoming Mr. Mishra and the other academicians, Mr. Nizamuddin said their joining was significant at a time when questions were being raised over the state of education and incidents of violence against students were being reported. He said Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi had been consistently fighting for justice for students and that the intellectual contribution of the new entrants would strengthen the Congress.
Mr. Yadav said the country’s youth and students needed “proper direction and guidance”, adding that better leadership was essential to securing the country’s future.
Mr. Gautam said the decision to join the Congress was aimed at protecting democracy, the Constitution and the education system. He said Mr. Mishra had consistently raised the concerns of professors and students.
Mr. Gautam also alleged that crores of rupees were being spent on BJP-RSS programmes at Delhi University, and said the money could instead have been used to build hostels and prevent incidents such as the recent collapse at Satya Niketan.
Mr. Mishra said he and his colleagues had joined the Congress to “strengthen Rahul Gandhi’s hands”. Government educational institutions across the country were “under attack”, he said, adding that thousands of schools had been shut down.
“Rahul Gandhi is fighting to uphold government-funded institutions, as well as justice and dignity for everybody,” Mr. Mishra said. The education system was “crumbling”, he said, adding that he and his colleagues had joined the struggle to help pull the country out of the crisis.
Ends

stories.headline: In 1905, Bengaluru residents paid Re 1 a month for a single electric bulb; how the city's electric journey began
stories.deck: Bengaluru received electricity from the Shivanasamudra hydroelectric station in 1905. The city's first electric streetlights illuminated areas near KR Market. Domestic connections rapidly increased, with 1,639 by June 1906. A single electric bulb cost one rupee monthly for residents then. This marked a significant transformation for the growing urban landscape.
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru residents today can power homes filled with lights, fans, appliances and gadgets with the flip of a switch. But more than a century ago, electricity was still a new and unfamiliar luxury in the city — and having a single electric bulb at home could cost just Re 1 a month. Bengaluru's electric-lighting story began in 1905, when the city became one of the first in India to receive electricity generated from a hydroelectric project. The power came from the Shivanasamudra hydroelectric station on the Cauvery, built primarily to supply electricity to the Kolar Gold Fields.
The first electric streetlights in Bengaluru were switched on in August 1905. The initial lighting was concentrated around areas including Siddikatte, near the present-day KR Market, before the network was gradually expanded to other parts of the city. The arrival of electricity transformed Bengaluru after sunset. Streets that had relied on older forms of lighting began getting electric lamps, while homes and businesses slowly started connecting to the new power supply.
A bulb at home cost Re 1 a month
Electricity did not remain limited to public streets for long. Residents began taking domestic connections, allowing electric bulbs to replace traditional forms of household lighting. By June 1906, Bengaluru had 1,639 domestic electric connections. 
The scale of the early network is striking when compared with the size of the city at the time. Electricity had moved from being a technological experiment to something thousands of households were beginning to use. Historical accounts put the monthly charge for a single electric bulb at Re 1. For residents living in Bengaluru in the early 1900s, that meant paying a fixed amount for something that today is taken for granted — lighting a room with electricity. The cost also reflected how electricity was initially treated as a new service rather than the basic household utility it would eventually become.
Electricity came from a hydro plant built for gold mines
There was another unusual connection behind Bengaluru's early electricity supply. The electricity illuminating Bengaluru's streets was generated at Shivanasamudra, hundreds of kilometres from the city. The hydroelectric project was established to supply power to the Kolar Gold Fields, where deep underground mines required electricity for operations. The Kolar Gold Fields had become a major gold-mining centre under British rule. Supplying electricity to the mines required a large and reliable source of power, leading to the development of the hydroelectric station on the Cauvery Bengaluru subsequently benefited from the same power network. This made the city's early electric-lighting story closely linked to two very different developments of the era: gold mining in Kolar and hydroelectric generation at Shivanasamudra.
From a few bulbs to a growing city
The rapid rise in domestic connections after the first streetlights showed how quickly Bengaluru embraced electricity. The city was already undergoing major changes at the time. The British Cantonment had developed separately from the older Pete, while new roads, institutions and neighbourhoods were expanding the urban landscape. Electricity became another marker of this transformation. The first streetlights were not simply about making roads brighter.
They represented the arrival of a new infrastructure that would eventually change how Bengaluru's homes, markets, factories and public spaces functioned. Within a year of the first electric lights, more than 1,600 domestic connections had been recorded. More than a century later, Bengaluru's relationship with electricity looks very different. The city now has a vast power network serving millions of residents and a technology-driven economy that depends heavily on uninterrupted electricity. But the story began with a much smaller network — and, for some residents, a single electric bulb that cost Re 1 a month. In 1905, Bengaluru was learning what it meant to have electric light. By 1906, thousands of households had already decided they wanted it inside their homes.

stories.headline: Bengaluru has jobs, weather and tech. Why is mobility becoming its weakest link?
stories.deck: Bengaluru offers jobs and weather, but mobility is a growing concern. Commuting times are unpredictable, impacting daily life and productivity significantly. While Namma Metro has expanded, it struggles with last-mile connectivity for many. BMTC buses carry the daily load, needing better integration with other transport modes. The city must build a connected mobility system to sustain its growth.
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Bengaluru has plenty going for it. It has the jobs, the technology industry, a huge startup ecosystem, a young workforce and weather that many other Indian metros can only envy. For years, these have helped make the city one of India's biggest magnets for professionals.
Last-mile connectivity remains a major gap
But there is a growing problem that threatens to take the shine off all these advantages: simply getting around the city. A recent viral video of a woman questioning what good Bengaluru's pleasant weather was if she could not step out because of traffic struck a chord with many residents. Her comparison with Hyderabad may have been casual, but it reflected a frustration that has become increasingly familiar to anyone who spends hours commuting across the city.
Read more:
‘What should I do with good weather?’: Woman prefers Hyderabad over Bengaluru traffic in viral video
When the commute becomes part of the problem
The problem with Bengaluru traffic is not merely that roads are crowded. It is that nobody can be quite sure how long a journey will take. A distance that looks manageable on a map can become an hour-long ordeal during peak hours, and a minor accident, road repair or sudden downpour can make matters worse. 
The pressure is particularly visible along the city's major employment corridors — the Outer Ring Road, Bellandur, Marathahalli, Silk Board, KR Puram, Whitefield and Electronic City. These are places where Bengaluru's economic success is most visible, but also where the mismatch between jobs and mobility is hardest to ignore.
Metro expansion hasn’t reduced traffic
Bengaluru has not ignored public transport. Namma Metro has expanded dramatically from its first 7-km stretch and now has around 96 km of operational network and 83 stations. Yet daily ridership is hovering around 10 lakh, well below the 30 lakh a day that had earlier been projected for the operational corridors.
Bengaluru’s traffic threatens its biggest advantages
That gap says something important. A metro line can take thousands of people off the road, but only if it is convenient for the journey people actually need to make. For someone living several kilometres from a station and working far from another, the Metro may still involve a bus, auto, bike or cab at either end. The private vehicle therefore remains the easier option for many commuters.
The last mile remains the missing piece
Bengaluru's mobility problem is, in many ways, a problem of connections. The city has Metro trains, BMTC buses, autos, cabs, two-wheelers and a growing range of app-based services. What it lacks is a seamless way of moving between them. A commuter may be perfectly willing to take the Metro but not if reaching the station means waiting for an unreliable bus or walking along a road with poor footpaths. The same problem appears after getting off the train. Unless the final few kilometres are convenient, safe and affordable, public transport will struggle to become the obvious choice. The question, therefore, should not be how many kilometres of Metro or how many buses the city has, but how easily a person can complete an entire journey.
BMTC still carries the city's daily load
That makes BMTC central to any serious solution. The bus network handles an estimated 35-42 lakh passenger trips a day, considerably more than the current Metro ridership. For a city of Bengaluru's size, buses can reach neighbourhoods and employment clusters that rail systems cannot cover on their own. The introduction of the One Karnataka Mobility App and WhatsApp-based bus ticketing is a useful step towards making public transport easier to access. But technology can only solve part of the problem. What matters on the ground is whether a commuter can find a bus quickly, whether it arrives on time and whether the connection to the next mode is reasonably smooth.
Managing traffic instead of solving it
Some of the city's recent traffic measures underline just how difficult the situation has become. Traffic authorities have experimented with restrictions for two-wheelers, autos and goods vehicles on selected elevated corridors and flyovers, while making changes when diversions create fresh bottlenecks. The experience on the airport corridor is a good example of the dilemma. Restricting one category of vehicle may ease pressure at one point, but if the diverted traffic spills onto nearby roads, congestion simply moves elsewhere. Bengaluru increasingly appears to be managing a shortage of road space rather than having enough efficient alternatives to private vehicles.
The cost is not just measured in minutes
There is also a larger economic question here. For Bengaluru's technology and services economy, commuting time is not simply an irritation at the end of a working day. It affects productivity, family life, employee satisfaction and even decisions about where companies locate offices. A person may move to Bengaluru for a well-paying technology job, but the calculation changes when that job comes with a daily commute of two hours each way. Infosys co-founder Kris Gopalakrishnan recently highlighted the problem by pointing to a 31-km journey that took 2.5 hours. When journeys of this kind become routine, traffic stops being a civic inconvenience and becomes a competitiveness issue for the city.
Can Bengaluru connect its own growth?
The answer is unlikely to come from one more flyover, one more road-widening project or one more traffic restriction. Bengaluru needs its Metro, BMTC buses, walking routes, cycling infrastructure, autos and other modes to work as parts of the same system. New roads can certainly ease particular bottlenecks, but every improvement that makes a corridor faster can also encourage more traffic to use it. The recent festive rush, when buses on the Bengaluru-Mangaluru route were delayed by up to three hours, offered another reminder of how quickly the transport network comes under pressure when travel demand rises.
Bengaluru's greatest strength has always been its ability to attract people looking for opportunity. That strength could become a weakness if the city becomes increasingly difficult to live in because of the time it takes to move around it. Bengaluru has the jobs, the technology and the weather. The challenge now is to build a mobility system that lets people enjoy those advantages instead of spending a large part of their day simply trying to get from one part of the city to another.

stories.headline: 529 child labourers rescued in Bengaluru; 105 cases registered
stories.bodyText:
As many as 529 child labourers were rescued and 105 cases registered against employers during a special operation conducted by the Bengaluru City Police on Saturday.
The operation was carried out on September 12 on the directions of senior police officers. Special teams comprising police personnel and Labour Department officials conducted surprise inspections at 6,076 commercial establishments, industrial areas and other locations across the city.
The rescued children were found working at different establishments, following which they were taken into the care of the authorities concerned for further action.
The police said 105 cases have so far been registered against shop owners and other employers who allegedly engaged children as labourers. The cases have been booked under provisions of the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act and the Juvenile Justice Act.
Among the city divisions, the West Division recorded the highest number of rescued children at 103, followed by north with 66, central with 63, south with 52 and north-east with 47.
The CCB rescued 45 children and registered the highest number of cases at 26, while the East Division rescued 74 children and registered 18 cases. The North-East Division registered 17 cases, while the west registered 15.
The police said the action against establishments employing children would continue.

stories.headline: 14 lakh groundwater irrigation sources identified in Karnataka
stories.bodyText:
The seventh Minor Irrigation Census and the second Census of Water Bodies in Karnataka have mapped nearly 39,000 lakes and water bodies that come under Minor Irrigation, and 14.18 lakh wells, including borewells and open wells, being used for agricultural activities, across the State.
While the wells mapped to tap underground water systems are for only agricultural activities (urban drinking water borewells not included), the 38,960 water bodies have covered up to 2,000 hectares of command areas. Besides, the Census has identified 77,573 surface water schemes, which include lift irrigation projects.
The data gathered in the Census was funded by the Union Ministry of Jal Shakti and uses 2023-24 as the reference year. The Census covered 30,671 villages, 300 urban local bodies, and 7,128 urban wards. More comparative data and findings of the Census would be available in the coming days, sources said.
“The field work of the Census, completed in August 2026, is aimed at assessing the actual status of the State’s water resources and enabling scientific planning for future irrigation and water conservation initiatives,” said Minor Irrigation and Science and Technology Minister Ajay Singh on Sunday.
“The data must be effectively used to prioritise water security interventions in drought-affected areas, rejuvenation of lakes, groundwater recharge, construction of check dams, and tank filling schemes. We will take steps towards the efficient management of the State’s water resources through data-driven planning and the use of technology,” he said in a press note.
According to the Minister, the data would help with identifying areas where water conservation interventions are most urgently required, where groundwater recharge must be prioritised, and where minor irrigation infrastructure needs to be strengthened.
Earlier in April, the 2025 Groundwater Assessment Report submitted to the government had shown that the overall groundwater extraction had reduced from 68.44% in 2024 to 66.49% in 2025, and the annual groundwater recharge capability had increased from 18.74 billion cubic meters (BCM) in 2024 to 19.28 billion cubic meters, while annual extractable groundwater resources rose from 16.88 BCM to 17.41 BCM.

briefs.headline: ‘What should I do with good weather?’: Woman prefers Hyderabad over Bengaluru traffic in viral video
briefs.deck: A digital creator has criticized Bengaluru's traffic congestion during her recent visit. She stated that travel within the city takes approximately two hours. The creator expressed her preference for Hyderabad over Bengaluru based on her experiences. She questioned the value of pleasant weather when mobility is severely limited. Her video criticizing the traffic has gained significant attention…
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU: A woman’s video criticising Bengaluru’s traffic has gone viral on Instagram, with her saying she has been “absolutely done” with the city’s congestion during her week-long stay.
Chetna Singh, a digital creator who identifies herself as a software engineer at Microsoft in Hyderabad, shared a reel saying it takes her around 1.5-2 hours to travel from one place to another in Bengaluru.
“Who says that Bangalore is better than Hyderabad?” she said in the video, adding that she is “absolutely freaking done” with the traffic.
Singh questioned the appeal of Bengaluru’s pleasant weather when travelling within the city takes so long.
“What should I do with the ‘good weather’ when I can’t go anywhere?” she said, before adding that she “just absolutely hate(s) the traffic here”.
Singh said she had been in Bengaluru for the past one week and compared her experience with Hyderabad, saying, “Hyderabad is far better than Bangalore; I’m absolutely loving it.”
Her Instagram caption also read: “Hyderabad is much better than Bangalore!!!”

briefs.headline: Firm’s cosmetic promise falls flat, Bengaluru woman wins Rs 1.8 lakh
briefs.deck: A woman was led to believe that a cosmetic procedure would yield guaranteed results; however, the clinic failed to provide the expected improvements. After she paid extra for a second treatment that was never carried out, she sought justice from a consumer forum. The ruling was clear: the clinic must refund her full payment and provide compensation for their failure to deliver.
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU: A visit to treat pigmentation turned into a costly ordeal for a Kadugodi resident after a clinic allegedly upsold her on an expensive cosmetic procedure, assuring her of guaranteed results that never materialised.
The IV additional district consumer disputes redressal commission has ordered a refund, holding that a firm promise of guaranteed results cannot be withdrawn after a consumer has paid for the procedure.
It all began in March 2025, when Sultana (name changed), a Kadugodi resident, approached the clinic for treatment of facial pigmentation. A representative recommended a package comprising ENNO Peeling and PRP (platelet-rich plasma) sessions.
During the consultation, clinic staff also recommended CoolSculpting, a non-invasive fat-reduction treatment.
Assured that the procedure would deliver effective results, Sultana underwent CoolSculpting on her upper abdomen at a cost of Rs 82,000. The treatment was financed through VLCC’s partner FIBE under an agreement signed on March 14.
When the treatment began on April 5, the technician handling her session allegedly told Sultana that treating only the upper abdomen would leave the results looking incomplete and uneven. 
She was therefore advised to undergo the procedure on her lower abdomen as well.
Acting on this advice, Sultana paid an additional Rs 82,000, taking her total payment to Rs 1.6 lakh.
The second payment was also financed through the same loan facility. She was assured that visible results would emerge within 90 days, by the end of May 2025.
However, even after the promised period had elapsed, Sultana saw no improvement. When she raised the issue with the clinic, VLCC allegedly acknowledged it and assured her of a repeat session. That session, however, was never provided.
Adding to her troubles, Sultana discovered that a “loan processing fee” of Rs 12,240 had also been charged to her. When she withheld an EMI payment in July 2025 in protest, she allegedly faced pressure and threats of legal action.
Her efforts to resolve the dispute through emails, personal visits and two complaints to National Consumer Helpline went largely unanswered.
A legal notice issued by her on Nov 1 was also returned unserved. Sultana then filed a consumer complaint on Dec 17, 2025, alleging deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.
In its defence, VLCC contended that the treatments had been performed in accordance with accepted cosmetology practices.
It argued that Sultana had voluntarily opted for the procedures and signed consent forms acknowledging that results could vary. The company also contended that she had produced no expert opinion establishing negligence.
The consumer forum observed that VLCC had not denied promising results within 90 days.
“Cosmetic procedures carry inherent biological variances, but the OP (opposite party) cannot commercially exploit a consumer by promising specific timelines only to back out later,” it noted.
The commission also found that after the first procedure failed, the clinic marketed a second, costlier treatment instead of offering a remedy or refund.
The bench, comprising president Ramachandra MS and members Nandini H Kumbhar and Savitha Airani, directed VLCC Ltd to refund Rs 1.7 lakh.
It also awarded Rs 10,000 for deficiency in service, Rs 3,000 for mental agony and hardship, and Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs.

briefs.headline: For 18 yrs, a Muslim woman has led Ganeshotsav in Karnataka's Chikkamagaluru
briefs.deck: Jubeeda, the panchayat president of Narasimharajapura's Muslim town, spearheads the Ganesh Chaturthi festivities, a role she has proudly held for the last eighteen years. The annual collaboration between Hindu and Muslim community members to install the Ganesha idol exemplifies a remarkable bond of unity. This celebration strengthens interfaith respect and highlights their shared values.
briefs.bodyText:
CHIKKAMAGALURU: This 
Ganesh Chaturthi
, a small town in coffee district of Chikkamagaluru is making waves of amity and harmony. Narasimharajapura town panchayat president Jubeeda, a Muslim, has been leading Ganeshotsav celebrations for 18 years as committee president, and she is all geared up for the festival on Monday.
Under the banner of Rajeeva Nagar Sri Vinayaka Seva Samiti, Jubeeda brings together both Hindu and Muslim communities to install the Ganesha idol at a pandal every year.
The committee conducts three days of puja, wraps it with a Satyanarayana puja before immersing the idol as has been the tradition for many years.
"I'm an Indian first. Religion and caste count much later. Along with my religion, I equally respect other religions. For me, humanity is above caste and religion. If we go for Hindu festivals in the town, they come and make Muslim festivals grand. All communities are living in harmony," Jubeeda, 52, said.
Jubeeda's secular spirit is not limited to Ganeshotsav. She works as office-bearer for Kartik Deepotsava (which is conducted around Deepavali) at Nagara Banashankari temple in the same locality of the town.
Her syncretic outlook has won praise from across the spectrum. 
"Jubeeda shares a cordial bond with people of all faiths and takes part in their joys and sorrows.
She actively participates in pujas and decorates her house with lamps during Deepavali. Those who sow seeds of poison between religions should learn from her," said HL Deepak, president, Vidya Ganesh Seva Samiti, Kudregundi, a village in the district.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru’s green brigade: Residents lead plogging in parks and plant herbs
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Citizens once again came together Sunday for a diverse set of activities under 
The Times of India
’s #IamBengaluru – Volunteer for Parks, presented by Multigen, in association with Kristu Jayanti University and supported by Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA).
The morning began with a plog run and waste segregation session at Madhavan Park in Jayanagar and Nagapura Park in Rajajinagar, organised in collaboration with Indian Ploggers Army and Youth For Seva, respectively. Volunteers across age groups collected sacks of plastic waste from the park and highlighted the importance of avoiding single-use plastics. The session ended with volunteers pledging to care for their surroundings.
Following the plogging session, the volunteers headed to Kempabudhi Park, which featured plantation activities. The session organised by Adamya Chetana foundation featured an eco-lifestyle talk and planting of medicinal herbs at the park. The team together planted shankupushpa creepers, rosemary, nagadali, lemongrass, nelabasale and vishamooli. The vine plantation was carried out to protect the park’s existing native flora.
Together, the activities reflected the movement’s continued focus on combining environmental action with community participation.
Participants SpeakAkash Mishra, resident of Haralur: This is my first time volunteering with 
TOI
. As we’re already seeing garbage everywhere, I wanted to do something about it. I collected all the waste materials from the park today; it even had glass from car windshields. I wanted to be involved with a group for a long time; this activity was also about educating ourselves. Earlier, even I used to throw away a lot of waste without realising it.
Inchara Swami, engineering student: We covered the entire perimeter of the park today and picked up microplastics. There were many cigarette and gutka packets. It’s my third week here; I’ll continue the activity in future too. We learnt the impact of plastic on the soil and how it is damaging as it doesn’t decompose.
Venkatesh Prasad, resident of SR Nagar: A huge number of our people don’t have proper civic sense; the litter here has come from all age groups. Children throw chocolate wrappers and adults throw alcohol bottles and gutka packets... I want the next generation to have better civic sense, I’m here for Gen Z.
Lalriatpui Molsom, resident of Jayanagar: I always like social activities; this is the second time I’ve joined the 
TOI
 initiative. Clean parks are very important for a peaceful mind. If you cannot achieve cleanliness through advice and awareness, we can at least show others and help them understand the value of clean parks. Seeing a clean park, I feel refreshed.
Dilip Kumar Mishra, resident of BTM Layout: Our environment is getting totally destroyed by population and vehicles, so definitely we have to come out of our homes; otherwise, our future will be affected. The biggest message of today’s activity is that people should take care of spaces near their homes and take responsibility. Instead of going somewhere else in the morning, we should do something for the betterment of environment and for clean oxygen near our homes.
Kumaraswamy S, Adamya Chetana member: The initiative is effective; today, we planted around 10 kinds of plants around the park. The message is that as nature and human beings coexist, we should not destroy nature and should instead be part of it and restore it. We need to plant as many trees as possible because every human needs at least 700kg of oxygen every year. A healthy tree can give 100kg of oxygen in a year; for each person, there should be seven trees; but it is not the case now.

briefs.headline: Enforcement Directorate director inBengaluru to review high-profile cases
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Enforcement Directorate
 (ED) director Rahul Navin and other senior officials arrived in Bengaluru from Delhi Saturday to review ongoing high-profile case investigations.
According to sources, the director held a meeting with senior officials at the agency’s office in Shanthinagar. The director is said to be in the city to review investigations into a few high-profile cases, including the recent raid linked to the minister for public works 
Satish Jarkiholi
 and the ongoing KPSC recruitment scam probe involving IAS officer Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar, KPSC officials and members, and middlemen in the recruitment of veterinary officers in an examination conducted by KPSC.
ED had recently conducted raids at multiple locations linked to Jarkiholi in connection with Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) violations.
ED is also probing Karnataka Maharshi Valmiki Scheduled Tribes Development Corporation (KMVSTDC) scam, in which former minister B Nagendra is an accused. Karnataka is among those having high-profile cases involving politicians and bureaucrats currently.
Navin refused to speak to the media at Kempegowda International Airport (KIA) after his arrival. ED officials have also not issued any official statement regarding the purpose of his visit. However, sources said that he is in the city to review the investigations.

briefs.headline: Audio advertisements coming soon to Bengaluru’s BMTC buses
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Those using buses for their everyday commute could soon be forced to listen to audio advertisements during their journey. Last week, Bangalore Metropolitan Transport Corporation (BMTC) floated a tender seeking an agency to run an in-bus audio advertisement system across its fleet.
In its initial phase, ads will be played in 300 non-AC BMTC buses across Bengaluru. The selected bidder will supply, install, operate and maintain the entire system — the first of its kind in South India. BMTC in the tender document stated that the primary objective of advertising is to generate non-fare revenue.
These advertisements will be spread across BMTC’s ordinary, express and night service buses, with each audio slot in Kannada lasting up to 10 seconds per minute. English translation can be optional. The fee will be charged per bus per month. The selected licensee will get a three-year contract, which could be extended further. Through this system, BMTC also plans to enable targeted location-based advertising by integrating it with existing GPS systems. Ads will be played in such a way that passenger announcements remain seamless without any interference.
About 10% of the advertising airtime will be reserved by BMTC for its own announcements, public service messages and authorised communications. 
The utility also plans to expand the service to more buses in future.
While BMTC assures that it will maintain passenger comfort through regulated volume, content quality and language compliance, commuters feel concerned it might impact their journeys. “During peak-hour travel, if these ads are noisy and start disturbing passengers, I feel this could lead to friction between them and the conductor. It should also not cause any hindrance to the stop announcements,” Rahul S, from the commuter group Friends of BMTC, said.
Akshay Bharadwaj K, a regular commuter from Magadi Road, said these ads could take a toll on passengers. “BMTC commuters already deal with a lot of noise, including honking, traffic sounds and chattering inside the bus. Playing ads will worsen the problem. I don’t want this to happen,” he added.

stories.headline: New costlier iPhones may boost refurbished smartphones' demand
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Apple's latest iPhone launch could trigger a fresh wave of trade-ins, while strengthening demand for older, refurbished models, as sharply higher flagship prices push buyers towards more affordable ways of entering the company's ecosystem, according to Cashify.
The refurbished-device platform expects buybacks to increase within 30 days of the launch and gather pace over the following 60-90 days as supplies improve, festive offers expand and more customers upgrade.
The iPhone 15 and iPhone 16 series are expected to record the strongest increase in buybacks. The iPhone 13 and 14 could continue contributing substantial volumes because of their larger installed base.
Apple accounted for 65.3% of refurbished smartphone sales on its platform in 2025 and 32.6% of all devices bought back. The iPhone 13 was both its bestselling refurbished iPhone and most frequently traded-in model. The iPhone 13 represented 6.93% of Cashify's smartphone buybacks but accounted for 15.5% of refurbished demand, indicating that demand exceeded the volume volume entering its resale system.
Meanwhile, refurbished-phone retailers expect demand for older iPhones to strengthen following the latest price increases, particularly among customers who want an Apple device but are unwilling to spend close to Rs 1 lakh on a new base model. 
Retailers also expect warranties, battery health and device certification to become more important as first-time buyers move towards the secondary market.
Higher supplies would ordinarily reduce prices of outgoing models. However, Cashify expects the elevated prices of new iPhones to simultaneously lift demand for previous generations, potentially limiting the correction. Prices could therefore soften gradually instead of declining sharply.
Demand is expected to shift progressively towards the iPhone 14 and 15 as availability improves, while the iPhone 16 may initially remain in the premium refurbished category because of its higher residual value.

stories.headline: AB InBev growth in India better than industry: Prez
stories.bodyText:
New Delhi: AB InBev, the world's largest brewer, has outpaced India's beer market in the first half of the year, making the country one of Budweiser's top three markets globally in June, behind US and China. The strong double-digit growth came despite the West Asia conflict, which disrupted supply chains and triggered can shortages, as premiumisation emerged as a key driver of beer consumption, Kartikeya Sharma, president, AB InBev India told TOI.
Premium beers grew about 20% during Jan-June, buoyed by regulatory changes in key markets, such as Maharashtra and Karnataka, helping the company gain share. While the industry grew around 12%, AB InBev grew faster, cornering about 20% share in the overall beer market of 20 million hectoliters in the first half.
The premium segment accounts for about 65% of the company's volumes, with brands including Budweiser, Corona and Hoegaarden key growth drivers.
Also, cans are becoming an increasingly important format in India's beer market, driven by convenience and portability, and account for about 28% of the overall beer market. The company's share is at over 40%, reflecting its sharper focus.
Further, beer category is thriving particularly in states where taxes have been normalised and there is a level-playing field between beer and spirits, with Maharashtra growing about 40%, he said. 
As against this, the hard spirits category seems to be declining.
Indicating a potential shift to moderation in consumer choice, Karnataka has emerged as a test case with the sale of beer below 5% ABV (alcohol by volume) doubling to 20% in three months. In May, it asked manufacturers to state alcohol content to the first decimal. In other states, beer may simply be categorised as above or below 5% alcohol.
"That encourages us to innovate around different consumer needs. A consumer may want a mid-week low-ABV beer at 2%, 2.5%, even 0%, depending on occasion. We lead the beer category globally and have examples in many markets where low-ABV products drive participation. Karnataka gives us the ability to test that thesis, and we intend to do so. Favorable policy should ultimately give consumers more choice, more variety, different price points'', Sharma stated.
"In the future, if there are opportunities, capabilities we want to bring in, or innovations we first want to test through the import route, those could be areas where we benefit,'' he added.

stories.headline: Govt. bars bank charges on payments up to ₹2,000 via UPI, RuPay-powered debit cards
stories.deck: The government notified changes ‌in the Payment And ​Settlement ⁠Act, 2007
stories.bodyText:
India on Monday (September 14, 2026) notified changes in the Payment And Settlement Act, 2007, specifying that banks cannot impose charges on payments via Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions of up to ₹2,000.
A government gazette notification specified RuPay-powered debit cards and UPI transactions of up to ₹2,000 as electronic modes of payment.
It said no bank or system provider shall impose any direct or indirect charge on a person making or receiving payments through these modes.
The notification altered an earlier provision that prevented banks from charging fees on digital payments via India’s popular UPI, paving the way for charges to be imposed on larger transfers.
A final decision on whether to introduce charges, and how they would be levied, has yet to be taken.

stories.headline: Maharashtra govt. orders probe into land transfer to Premier Automobiles over six decades ago
stories.deck: Following allegations of cattle-grazing land allotted for industrial purpose in 1960s turning into premium real estate in alleged land use violation, the Maharashtra Revenue Department has constituted a nine-member Special Investigation Team (SIT), headed by the Konkan Divisional Commissioner
stories.bodyText:
An investigation has been ordered into the allotment of about 175 acres land by Maharashtra government to Premier Automobile Ltd (Now renamed Premier Ltd) more than six decades ago and the subsequent transfer of land parcels by the company to real estate developers and other entities.
Premier Automobiles was synonymous with the iconic Fiat 1100 D, the Premier Padmini car as well as Premier 118NE.
Following allegations of cattle-grazing land allotted for industrial purpose in 1960s turning into premium real estate in alleged land use violation, the Maharashtra Revenue Department has constituted a nine-member Special Investigation Team (SIT), headed by the Konkan Divisional Commissioner, to examine the alleged transfer of government-owned grazing land in Kalyan taluka, Thane district near Mumbai.
The government order, issued on September 4, follows directions given at a meeting chaired by Revenue Minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule on August 19, 2026.
The Minister was hearing complaints concerning parcels of cattle-grazing land in Mangaon, Kole, Katai, Gharivali, Sandap and Usarghar villages. The complaints trace the original transactions to 1960s the period when Maharashtra was seeking to promote industrialisation and attract manufacturing activity.
Premier Automobiles, one of the pioneers in automobile assembling belonging to the Walchand Group, was then expanding from it’s original factory in Kurla in Suburban Mumbai to this location in Kalyan-Dombivali.
SIT to scrutinise government and grazing-land records
The SIT has been asked to scrutinise original government and grazing-land records and examine transfers made through gram panchayats to Premier Automobiles and then to other entities.
These include Lodha Developers, Anant Developers and Jupiter Life Line Hospital. A separate term dealing with third-party sales names Out N Out Infotech and Sundarniwas Properties.
These land parcels were previously owned by Premier Automobiles and later monetised to repay debt and to invest in it’s plant in Pune.
Inquiry to cover five broad issues
The inquiry will cover five broad issues: the original status of the land and manner of transfer; conversion of parcels from Occupant Class II to Occupant Class I; the validity of entries in the record of rights, including 7/12 extracts and mutation entries; subsequent sale transactions; and action to be recommended if responsibility is established.
The SIT has also been asked to examine whether the conversion of tenure and the calculation or adjustment of the unearned amount payable to the government complied with applicable orders and rules.
It must determine whether any government land was encroached upon or whether official powers were misused.
The SIT has been tasked to conduct an in-depth scrutiny of all documents and records of rights and will submit to the Government a detailed final report containing its clear opinion and recommendations in the first week of October 2026.
The SIT investigation is considered significant beyond the specific 175-acre Kalyan case as it could establish a precedent for reviewing old industrial land allotments and subsequent use for commercial development and monetisation.
